[THOUGHT]  
The critical finding is severe, isolated upper-extremity hypertension (150/80 mm Hg) in a 5-year-old boy with a documented *lower* blood pressure in the lower extremities — a classic inter-arm and arm–leg BP gradient. This pattern is highly specific for **coarctation of the aorta**, a congenital narrowing of the aortic lumen typically distal to the left subclavian artery. In children, coarctation commonly presents with upper-body hypertension, weak or delayed femoral pulses, and differential blood pressures — all implied here (upper > lower BP, prompting concern for coarctation as the leading explanation). While renal artery stenosis or other secondary causes (e.g., pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome) can cause childhood hypertension, they rarely produce such a pronounced *arm–leg gradient*; moreover, they are far less common than coarctation in this age group with no systemic symptoms (e.g., headache, sweating, weight gain, hypokalemia). The absence of growth data or labs does not weaken the hemodynamic clue — the BP gradient itself is a direct physical sign of obstructive aortopathy. Echocardiography is the gold-standard initial test for coarctation in children and would confirm discrete narrowing, post-stenotic dilation, and collateral flow — all expected. No other diagnosis explains the magnitude of elevation *plus* the directional gradient so parsimoniously.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Blood pressure 150/80 mm Hg in right upper extremity — severely elevated for age (95th percentile ≈ 105/65 mm Hg).  
- Lower extremity BP values are *lower* than upper extremity — establishing an arm–leg systolic and diastolic gradient.
